nodes.name: Medieval music
nodes.description: Western sacred and secular music of the medieval era: chant, troubadour song, and early polyphony. Dates delimit a historical era, not the end of its living repertoire.

nodes.name: Renaissance music
nodes.description: Interwoven vocal polyphony, masses, motets, and madrigals in Renaissance Europe. Era boundaries are approximate; the repertoire is still performed.

nodes.name: Baroque music
nodes.description: Basso continuo, opera, concertos, and contrapuntal invention. Approximate dates mark the historical era, not the disappearance of Baroque performance.

nodes.name: Classical era
nodes.description: The Classical period, not the umbrella term classical music: balanced phrases, sonata form, symphonies, and string quartets. Its historical boundaries overlap the Romantic era.

nodes.name: Romantic music
nodes.description: Expanded orchestras, expressive harmony, virtuoso soloists, and musical storytelling. Dates describe a historical era whose repertoire remains active.

nodes.name: Modern classical
nodes.description: An umbrella for modern and contemporary Western art music, from impressionism and modernism to experimental composition. Not a single unified style.

nodes.name: Minimalism
nodes.description: Repetition, sustained tones, gradual processes, and shifting patterns in experimental composition. One strand of modern classical music, with a reach into rock and electronic music.

nodes.name: Blues
nodes.description: African American musical traditions shaped by expressive vocal phrasing, blue notes, and recurring harmonic forms. A major source for jazz, rhythm and blues, and rock and roll.

nodes.name: Jazz
nodes.description: African American music emerging in New Orleans around the turn of the twentieth century, built on improvisation, rhythmic interplay, and blues traditions. The umbrella for many distinct jazz styles.

nodes.name: Swing
nodes.description: A jazz style and dance-music idiom built around swinging rhythms, arranged sections, and improvisation, performed by large bands and smaller groups. It became the dominant U.S. popular-music form in the 1930s and 1940s, while later swing traditions continued in different settings.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate U.S. popular-music visibility: the Library of Congress and Philadelphia jazz histories place swing and the big-band era at the center of popular music from the 1930s into the mid-1940s. Swing continued as a practice after its period of national dominance; these are not worldwide measurements.

nodes.name: Bebop
nodes.description: Small-group jazz with fast tempos, intricate melodies, and improvisation over rapidly moving chord changes. A foundational language of modern jazz.

nodes.name: Cool jazz
nodes.description: Restrained dynamics, lighter timbres, and carefully arranged textures in postwar jazz. Includes, but is not synonymous with, West Coast jazz.

nodes.name: Hard bop
nodes.description: Bebop extended through blues, gospel, and rhythm-and-blues phrasing, with a strong groove and earthy ensemble sound.

nodes.name: Modal jazz
nodes.description: Improvisation organized around modes and longer harmonic spaces rather than dense sequences of chord changes.

nodes.name: Free jazz
nodes.description: Jazz that experiments with or abandons fixed chord progressions, regular meter, and conventional ensemble roles in favor of freer improvisation.

nodes.name: Jazz fusion
nodes.description: Jazz improvisation meets rock amplification, electric instruments, and funk rhythms. An evolving family of approaches rather than a single formula.

nodes.name: Rock and roll
nodes.description: A mid-20th-century popular style formed through African American rhythm and blues, country, gospel, and other regional traditions. It reached broad youth and national audiences in the United States in the mid-1950s, while its roots and early contributors predate that commercial breakthrough.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate U.S. popular-music visibility: related Black and country traditions predate the mid-1950s, when rock and roll reached broad national and youth audiences. The phases mark that commercial breakthrough and subsequent diversification, not the invention of its roots or a global popularity curve.

nodes.name: Rock
nodes.description: A broad family of popular music that grew from mid-century rock and roll into many guitar-centered and electronic, vocal, and studio-based forms. It overlaps with, but is not identical to, the narrower early rock-and-roll category.

nodes.name: Blues rock
nodes.description: Electric blues vocabulary played with rock volume and rhythm, often emphasizing guitar solos and extended improvisation.

nodes.name: Psychedelic rock
nodes.description: Rock expanded through studio experimentation, unusual timbres, long improvisations, and the counterculture of the 1960s.

nodes.name: Progressive rock
nodes.description: Rock explored through extended forms, shifting meters, concept albums, and elements of classical music and jazz.

nodes.name: Hard rock
nodes.description: Heavy guitar riffs, forceful drums, and powerful vocals grew out of blues and garage rock into a durable arena and club sound.

nodes.name: Heavy metal
nodes.description: Amplified heaviness, distortion, emphatic riffs, and dramatic performance developed from late-1960s hard rock.

nodes.name: Punk rock
nodes.description: Short, urgent songs and a do-it-yourself ethos challenged rock spectacle and helped establish independent musical networks.

nodes.name: Post-punk
nodes.description: Punk's independence redirected into experimental structures, angular guitars, and influences from dub, funk, and electronic music.

nodes.name: Alternative rock
nodes.description: An umbrella for rock scenes and artists working through independent labels, college radio, and other routes outside the mainstream. In the United States, grunge and other alternative acts broke into mass-market visibility in the early 1990s; the label continued to cover diverse sounds afterward.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate U.S. mainstream visibility: alternative rock moved from underground and college-radio networks into mass-market attention in the early 1990s, with grunge one major route rather than the whole genre. This describes a market shift, not a single creative peak or an international ranking.

nodes.name: Grunge
nodes.description: A Pacific Northwest scene and style whose bands drew on punk, metal, and other rock traditions. Sub Pop’s local releases and Nirvana’s 1991 “Nevermind” helped bring some Seattle-area music to international mainstream attention; grunge was never a single sound or the whole region’s music.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate U.S. and international mainstream visibility: a local Pacific Northwest scene preceded the early-1990s breakthrough, which “Nevermind” helped accelerate; the scene and its artists continued in varied directions after the commercial peak. These are not all-artist or global popularity dates.

nodes.name: Hildegard of Bingen
nodes.description: Medieval composer of sacred monophonic songs and the music drama Ordo Virtutum. Dates approximate her documented composing period, not her lifespan.

nodes.name: Léonin
nodes.description: Notre-Dame school composer associated with early polyphonic organum. Activity dates are approximate because biographical evidence is limited.

nodes.name: Pérotin
nodes.description: Notre-Dame school composer known for large-scale polyphonic organum. Dates indicate an approximate period of activity.

nodes.name: Josquin des Prez
nodes.description: Renaissance composer of masses, motets, and secular vocal works.

nodes.name: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
nodes.description: Italian Renaissance composer celebrated for sacred vocal polyphony.

nodes.name: William Byrd
nodes.description: English composer of sacred polyphony, consort music, and keyboard works.

nodes.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
nodes.description: German Baroque composer whose sacred, orchestral, and keyboard works unite intricate counterpoint with expressive harmony.

nodes.name: George Frideric Handel
nodes.description: Baroque composer of operas, oratorios, and instrumental music, with a career centered in London.

nodes.name: Antonio Vivaldi
nodes.description: Venetian Baroque composer and violinist, especially associated with the solo concerto.

nodes.name: Joseph Haydn
nodes.description: Classical composer central to the development of the symphony and string quartet.

nodes.name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
nodes.description: Classical composer of operas, concertos, symphonies, and chamber music, active from childhood.

nodes.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
nodes.description: Composer whose symphonies, sonatas, and quartets bridge Classical forms and Romantic expression.

nodes.name: Frédéric Chopin
nodes.description: Romantic composer and pianist who transformed the expressive language of solo piano music.

nodes.name: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
nodes.description: Romantic composer of symphonies, operas, concertos, and ballet scores.

nodes.name: Claude Debussy
nodes.description: French composer whose colors and harmonic innovations helped reshape music at the turn of the twentieth century.

nodes.name: Arnold Schoenberg
nodes.description: Modernist composer associated with atonality and the development of twelve-tone composition.

nodes.name: Igor Stravinsky
nodes.description: Composer whose career spans Russian ballets, neoclassicism, and serial works. The end marks his last completed compositions.

nodes.name: Steve Reich
nodes.description: American composer known for phasing, repeating patterns, and gradual musical processes.

nodes.name: Philip Glass
nodes.description: American composer whose repetitive structures extend across ensemble works, operas, and film scores.

nodes.name: Terry Riley
nodes.description: American composer whose In C helped establish a flexible, repeating-pattern approach to minimalism.

nodes.name: Robert Johnson
nodes.description: Delta blues singer and guitarist whose small recorded catalogue became influential in later blues and rock.

nodes.name: Muddy Waters
nodes.description: Singer and guitarist central to the amplified Chicago blues sound.

nodes.name: B.B. King
nodes.description: Blues singer and guitarist celebrated for lyrical phrasing and an expressive single-note guitar style.

nodes.name: Louis Armstrong
nodes.description: New Orleans trumpeter and singer whose improvisation helped make the jazz soloist central to the music.

nodes.name: Duke Ellington
nodes.description: Pianist, bandleader, and composer whose orchestra expanded jazz's expressive and structural possibilities.

nodes.name: Jelly Roll Morton
nodes.description: New Orleans pianist, bandleader, and composer associated with early jazz arrangements.

nodes.name: Count Basie
nodes.description: Pianist and bandleader whose Kansas City swing emphasized blues phrasing and rhythmic economy.

nodes.name: Benny Goodman
nodes.description: Clarinetist and bandleader prominent in the swing era.

nodes.name: Charlie Parker
nodes.description: Alto saxophonist whose melodic and harmonic innovations were central to bebop.

nodes.name: Dizzy Gillespie
nodes.description: Trumpeter and composer central to bebop and the development of Afro-Cuban jazz.

nodes.name: Thelonious Monk
nodes.description: Pianist and composer with a distinctive rhythmic and harmonic language, associated with the emergence of bebop.

nodes.name: Miles Davis
nodes.description: Trumpeter and bandleader whose changing ensembles helped shape cool jazz, modal jazz, and electric fusion.

nodes.name: Dave Brubeck
nodes.description: Pianist and composer associated with cool jazz and experiments in unusual meters.

nodes.name: Chet Baker
nodes.description: Trumpeter and singer known for the lyrical, restrained sound of West Coast cool jazz.

nodes.name: Art Blakey
nodes.description: Drummer whose Jazz Messengers became a defining hard-bop ensemble and a training ground for younger musicians.

nodes.name: Horace Silver
nodes.description: Pianist and composer who brought blues and gospel inflections to hard bop.

nodes.name: Clifford Brown
nodes.description: Trumpeter whose work with Max Roach is a landmark of early hard bop.

nodes.name: John Coltrane
nodes.description: Saxophonist whose work moved from bebop and hard bop into modal and freer improvisation.

nodes.name: McCoy Tyner
nodes.description: Pianist associated with John Coltrane's quartet and a powerful modal harmonic language.

nodes.name: Ornette Coleman
nodes.description: Saxophonist and composer whose late-1950s ensembles helped establish free jazz.

nodes.name: Cecil Taylor
nodes.description: Pianist and composer known for percussive intensity and freely structured improvisation.

nodes.name: Albert Ayler
nodes.description: Saxophonist whose forceful, spiritually charged playing became central to 1960s free jazz.

nodes.name: Weather Report
nodes.description: Electric jazz-fusion group founded by Joe Zawinul and Wayne Shorter.

nodes.name: Mahavishnu Orchestra
nodes.description: John McLaughlin's fusion ensemble combined jazz improvisation, rock intensity, and complex rhythmic structures; activity included multiple lineups and breaks.

nodes.name: Chuck Berry
nodes.description: Guitarist and songwriter whose riffs and storytelling helped define rock and roll.

nodes.name: Little Richard
nodes.description: Singer and pianist whose explosive voice and driving rhythm became foundational to rock and roll.

nodes.name: Elvis Presley
nodes.description: Singer whose early recordings brought country and rhythm-and-blues influences to a mass rock-and-roll audience.

nodes.name: The Beatles
nodes.description: Liverpool band whose songwriting and studio experiments reshaped rock and pop.

nodes.name: The Rolling Stones
nodes.description: British band that developed a blues-based sound into one of rock's longest-running careers.

nodes.name: The Who
nodes.description: British rock band known for forceful live performance, ambitious songwriting, and rock operas.

nodes.name: Cream
nodes.description: British power trio central to blues rock. Original activity ran 1966-1968, with reunion performances in 1993 and 2005; the career envelope includes those breaks.

nodes.name: Jimi Hendrix
nodes.description: Guitarist and songwriter who expanded amplified blues and psychedelic rock through feedback, effects, and improvisation.

nodes.name: Grateful Dead
nodes.description: San Francisco band associated with psychedelic rock and long-form concert improvisation.

nodes.name: Jefferson Airplane
nodes.description: San Francisco psychedelic-rock band. Original activity ran 1965-1972, with a 1989 reunion and a final 1996 appearance; dates include those breaks.

nodes.name: Yes
nodes.description: Progressive-rock group known for extended compositions, virtuoso playing, and changing lineups.

nodes.name: King Crimson
nodes.description: Progressive-rock band with an evolving combination of complex meters, improvisation, and experimental textures. Career dates include extended breaks.

nodes.name: Genesis
nodes.description: British band that developed from theatrical progressive rock into a broader pop-rock sound, with multiple hiatuses and reunions.

nodes.name: Led Zeppelin
nodes.description: British band whose blues-based riffs helped define hard rock. Original activity ended in 1980; dates include later one-off reunions, most recently in 2007.

nodes.name: Deep Purple
nodes.description: British hard-rock band known for heavy riffs and classically inflected keyboards; its history includes a 1976-1984 breakup.

nodes.name: AC/DC
nodes.description: Australian band built on blues-derived riffs and a direct, driving hard-rock sound.

nodes.name: Black Sabbath
nodes.description: Birmingham band whose dark, heavy riffs helped establish heavy metal. Dates include breaks and the final 2025 reunion performance.

nodes.name: Judas Priest
nodes.description: British heavy-metal band known for twin-guitar arrangements and powerful vocals.

nodes.name: Iron Maiden
nodes.description: British heavy-metal band associated with galloping rhythms, harmonized guitars, and long-form storytelling.

nodes.name: Ramones
nodes.description: New York band whose fast, concise songs became a blueprint for punk rock.

nodes.name: Sex Pistols
nodes.description: British punk band whose original 1975-1978 run became culturally defining. The career envelope includes sporadic reunions and a later lineup.

nodes.name: The Clash
nodes.description: British punk band that incorporated reggae, dub, rockabilly, and other musical forms.

nodes.name: Joy Division
nodes.description: Manchester post-punk band known for stark arrangements and a brooding atmosphere.

nodes.name: Talking Heads
nodes.description: New York band combining art-school experimentation, punk-era independence, and funk-influenced rhythm.

nodes.name: The Cure
nodes.description: British band emerging from post-punk, with a catalogue ranging from stark gothic textures to pop.

nodes.name: R.E.M.
nodes.description: Athens, Georgia band whose independent-label beginnings and college-radio following helped define alternative rock.

nodes.name: Sonic Youth
nodes.description: New York band bringing alternate tunings, noise, and experimental guitar textures into alternative rock.

nodes.name: Pixies
nodes.description: American alternative-rock band known for sharp loud-quiet contrasts. Dates include a 1993-2004 breakup.

nodes.name: Nirvana
nodes.description: Washington band whose Nevermind brought grunge and alternative rock to a mass audience.

nodes.name: Pearl Jam
nodes.description: Seattle rock band associated with the early-1990s grunge breakthrough.

nodes.name: Soundgarden
nodes.description: Seattle band combining heavy riffs and unusual meters. Dates include the 1997-2010 breakup, the 2017 dissolution, and occasional reunion performances through September 2026; they do not imply continuous activity.

nodes.name: Soul
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate U.S. recording and crossover visibility: soul became a major Black popular-music category in the 1960s, with a broad mid-1960s peak; later soul and neo-soul scenes renewed the style. These are editorial periods, not measured chart rankings or a global popularity curve.
nodes.description: A Black American popular-music family formed through gospel and rhythm-and-blues practices, with distinct label, regional, and studio traditions. Soul became a prominent crossover style in the 1960s; later artists continued to rework its vocal and musical approaches.

nodes.name: Funk
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate U.S. popular-record visibility: funk became a widely popular dance-music form in the 1970s, then many traditional bands receded from the mainstream in the early 1980s while funk persisted through new production and hip-hop sampling. Scene activity and influence continued beyond the high-visibility period; not a measured global ranking.
nodes.description: A rhythm-centered Black American music family developed by artists and bands in the 1960s and popularized widely in the 1970s. It includes distinct regional and band styles, and its bass, drum, and horn patterns continued to circulate through later R&B and hip-hop sampling.

nodes.name: Disco
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate U.S. mainstream and club visibility: the mid-to-late 1970s brought disco’s mass-market peak and backlash; club scenes and related music continued afterward, with later disco revivals. A single U.S. backlash date does not mark the genre’s end, and the shading is not a global chart measure.
nodes.description: A dance-music family shaped in 1970s club networks, especially in New York and Philadelphia, by Black, Latino, and LGBTQ communities and by producers working across soul, funk, and orchestral pop. Club DJ practice, extended mixes, and the 12-inch single became important to its circulation; its histories continued after the U.S. backlash of 1979.

nodes.name: Hip-hop
nodes.description: A musical and cultural movement that developed in New York’s Bronx during the 1970s, shaped by Black and Puerto Rican communities and Caribbean diasporic practices. DJing, MCing, dance, visual art, and later regional rap scenes are connected but distinct parts of its history.
nodes.phaseNote: The late-1980s and 1990s “Golden Age” is a documented U.S.-centered cultural and critical period, not an uncontested global peak or a claim that hip-hop stopped changing afterward. Shading combines broad U.S. public visibility and historical periodization; it is not a sales or streaming series.

nodes.name: Krautrock
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative shading of the West German scene’s activity and later international rediscovery, not mainstream popularity: the original scene is concentrated in the late 1960s and early-to-mid-1970s; renewed reception followed from the mid-1990s onward. No measured popularity series is implied.
nodes.description: West German experimental rock — motorik repetition and early synthesizers. The laboratory Kraftwerk emerged from.

nodes.name: Synth-pop
nodes.description: Pop-oriented electronic music in which synthesizers and electronic production are prominent, alongside voices, guitars, drums, and other instruments. The style emerged across several scenes in the late 1970s and early 1980s; Kraftwerk and British new wave acts were influential, but neither alone defines it.

nodes.name: Italo disco
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate international-market and specialist-scene visibility: research places the genre’s initial peak in the first half of the 1980s; later reissues, DJ circulation, and retro revivals renewed attention from the 2000s. The domestic Italian and international naming histories differ, so this is not a national or global sales curve.
nodes.description: An Italian-centered post-disco dance music that took shape through electronic records and independent production in the early 1980s, with an international market and circulation through DJs and wholesalers. “Italo disco” became a category abroad before it became a common self-description in Italy; later reissues and revivals reshaped its reputation.

nodes.name: Hi-NRG
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate North American club and UK chart visibility: Hi-NRG moved from queer club scenes into a wider pop period in the 1980s, with trade charts and UK crossover records documenting the high-visibility years. Sources differ on the exact peak and on how Hi-NRG relates to Eurobeat and Italo disco; no worldwide popularity measure is implied.
nodes.description: A high-tempo, synthesizer-led development of disco associated with North American queer club culture and later UK pop production. Its visibility varied by territory: specialist club and trade charts, crossover singles, and later dance styles document different parts of its history.

nodes.name: Electro
nodes.description: An electronic dance style shaped by electro-funk and hip-hop, using drum machines, synthesized bass, and sometimes vocoders or other processed voices. “Planet Rock” was a landmark recording; Detroit groups such as Cybotron developed related but distinct local approaches.

nodes.name: Chicago house
nodes.description: A house style and club practice that developed in Chicago in the early to mid-1980s. DJs and producers reshaped disco, soul, and electronic records with drum machines, sequencers, and studio edits; the Warehouse is central to the history, while the exact etymology of “house” is not settled by one account.

nodes.name: Garage house
nodes.description: A New York house lineage associated with the Paradise Garage and DJ Larry Levan, where house, disco, soul, gospel, and extended DJ mixing overlapped. The label describes a scene and a range of records rather than a single fixed sound.

nodes.name: Deep house
nodes.description: A Chicago-associated house style that often uses spacious arrangements, deeper bass, jazz- and soul-inflected harmony, and understated vocals. Larry Heard is a central early figure, but the style grew through multiple producers and club networks.

nodes.name: Acid house
nodes.description: A house style in which the resonant filter sweeps of the Roland TB-303 became a defining sound; Phuture’s “Acid Tracks” was a pivotal early recording. Chicago records reached the UK through DJs and clubs, where acid house helped drive a distinct late-1980s rave movement.

nodes.name: Detroit techno
nodes.description: A regional form of techno developed by Detroit-area artists from the early to mid-1980s. Its history includes the Belleville Three, other Detroit producers and labels, Black radio and club culture, and exchanges with Chicago and Europe.

nodes.name: Minimal techno
nodes.description: A techno approach built around sparse materials, repetition, and small changes over time. Detroit figures including Robert Hood and Daniel Bell helped establish an influential early-1990s strand; later scenes developed distinct versions.

nodes.name: Dub techno
nodes.description: A techno and dub synthesis associated especially with Berlin’s Basic Channel releases in the early 1990s. Long delays, reverberation, filtering, and reduced rhythmic material make space and decay part of the composition.

nodes.name: Trance
nodes.description: A family of electronic dance music styles built around sustained rhythmic motion and extended, often melodic development. Early German scenes, including Frankfurt, were important to its formation, alongside wider European club networks.

nodes.name: Gabber
nodes.description: A Dutch hardcore dance style that emerged around Rotterdam in the early 1990s, marked by fast tempos, forceful kick drums, and deliberately distorted production. Its history belongs to the wider European hardcore continuum.

nodes.name: Breakbeat hardcore
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate UK rave-scene visibility: the style was prominent in the early-1990s rave period before the scene fragmented into related branches; later revivals are specialist rather than a return to the same national mainstream position. These are scene markers, not attendance or sales statistics.
nodes.description: An early-1990s UK rave style combining house and acid-house structures with chopped breakbeats, sampling, and influences circulating through hip-hop and sound-system culture. As the rave scene fragmented, related strands developed into jungle, darkcore, and happy hardcore.

nodes.name: Jungle
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate UK scene and media visibility: jungle’s early-1990s breakthrough and mid-decade move into broader radio attention are documented, followed by a long specialist presence and renewed 2010s/2020s interest. Visibility differed across pirate radio, clubs, charts, and countries; this is not a global popularity score.
nodes.description: A Black British club and sound-system formation that grew from the UK rave continuum in the early 1990s, bringing breakbeat programming into dialogue with Jamaican sound-system practices, reggae and dancehall bass, and pirate radio. It developed into multiple branches and later drum-and-bass scenes.

nodes.name: Drum and bass
nodes.description: A broad UK-rooted family of fast breakbeat dance music that developed through the mid-1990s rave and jungle continuum. The name and sound came to cover varied branches rather than one “refined” successor style.

nodes.name: UK garage
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate UK chart and club visibility: scene growth in the mid-1990s, chart breakthrough around the turn of the millennium, and later revival waves are documented by charts and specialist histories. These intervals describe UK visibility, not the genre’s worldwide popularity or the persistence of its underground scenes.
nodes.description: A London-centered dance style that developed in the mid-1990s from circulating US garage records and UK club, pirate-radio, and rave practices. Speed garage and 2-step brought different rhythms and production choices; later branches include grime and dubstep, without making them interchangeable genres.

nodes.name: Dubstep
nodes.description: A South London style that coalesced in the early 2000s through garage-related club networks, with sparse arrangements, sub-bass, and varied references to dub, reggae, and rave. Its later international branches changed the sound substantially; Croydon is an important scene, not a complete origin story.

nodes.name: Kraftwerk
nodes.description: Düsseldorf's man-machines. 'Trans-Europe Express' and 'Computer World' are cited by Juan Atkins and Afrika Bambaataa alike as the source code.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence anchored to Autobahn, Trans-Europe Express, Computer World, and the 2003 Tour de France Soundtracks return. This describes recording-era visibility, not the continuing magnitude of Kraftwerk's influence or measured listening.

nodes.name: Giorgio Moroder
nodes.description: Munich producer whose fully sequenced 'I Feel Love' (1977) proved electronic dance music could be the future, not a gimmick.

nodes.name: Juan Atkins
nodes.description: Detroit producer and DJ whose work with Cybotron and as Model 500 helped shape early techno. Atkins used the word “techno” for Cybotron’s music before it became a name for the Detroit style; he was one of the Belleville Three and founded Metroplex.

nodes.name: Derrick May
nodes.description: Detroit DJ and producer, one of the Belleville Three. Recording as Rhythim Is Rhythim, he released “Strings of Life” on his Transmat label; his work and touring helped carry Detroit techno to international audiences.

nodes.name: Kevin Saunderson
nodes.description: Detroit DJ and producer, one of the Belleville Three. He founded KMS Records and produced house and techno releases as well as the charting project Inner City.

nodes.name: Belleville Three
nodes.description: Atkins, May, and Saunderson — high-school friends from Belleville, Michigan, who invented Detroit techno between mixtapes and Metroplex.

nodes.name: Cybotron
nodes.description: The Detroit electronic group formed around Juan Atkins and Richard “3070” Davis, with Jon-5 joining later. Its early singles, including “Clear” and “Techno City,” connect electro, funk, and the emerging Detroit techno vocabulary; the project later resumed recording.

nodes.name: Frankie Knuckles
nodes.description: The Godfather of House. His edits and drum-machine experiments as Warehouse resident birthed the genre that took the club's name.

nodes.name: Ron Hardy
nodes.description: Music Box resident whose raw, manic sets made Chicago's wildest records — he broke 'Acid Tracks' from a cassette.

nodes.name: Larry Levan
nodes.description: Paradise Garage resident; his eclectic, emotional marathon sets defined garage house and modern DJ culture.

nodes.name: Phuture
nodes.description: DJ Pierre, Spanky, and Herb J. Twisting a TB-303's knobs past reason, they invented acid house with 'Acid Tracks'.

nodes.name: Jeff Mills
nodes.description: The Wizard. Co-founded Underground Resistance, then defined hard minimal techno on Axis and early Tresor.

nodes.name: Underground Resistance
nodes.description: Detroit music collective and record label whose releases linked techno production with independent infrastructure and political expression. Its contributors and roster changed over time; anonymity and collective presentation are recurring parts of its public identity.

nodes.name: Richie Hawtin
nodes.description: Windsor's Plastikman, across the river from Detroit. Stripped acid and techno down to minimal's blueprint.

nodes.name: Carl Craig
nodes.description: Second-wave Detroit polymath, May's protégé — stretched techno toward jazz and orchestras on Planet E.

nodes.name: Goldie
nodes.description: Graffiti writer turned jungle auteur. 'Timeless' and his Metalheadz label took drum and bass to the world.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence centered on the early jungle singles and the 1995 Timeless breakthrough, followed by ongoing production and later releases. This is scene-relative editorial shading, not a ranking against mainstream artists or measured listening.

nodes.name: Metroplex
nodes.description: Detroit label founded by Juan Atkins in 1985. It released Model 500’s “No UFOs,” a seminal early techno record, and helped establish the independent label network around Detroit’s first techno generation.

nodes.name: Transmat
nodes.description: Derrick May's label. 'Strings of Life' and the Transmat seal: emotional futurism from Detroit.

nodes.name: KMS
nodes.description: Kevin Saunderson's label, bridge between Detroit techno and the global charts via Inner City.

nodes.name: Trax Records
nodes.description: Chicago's chaotic house factory — 'Acid Tracks', 'Your Love', and most of the genre's canon on recycled vinyl.

nodes.name: Tresor
nodes.description: Berlin club and label in a bank vault under Potsdamer Platz; the Detroit–Berlin axis made concrete after the Wall fell.

nodes.name: Detroit
nodes.description: Michigan city and a central site in the development of techno. The history includes Black radio and club culture, local producers and independent labels, and transnational exchanges that later shaped scenes elsewhere.

nodes.name: Chicago
nodes.description: Where disco survived its backlash underground and mutated into house.

nodes.name: New York
nodes.description: Birthplace of disco DJ culture, hip-hop, and the Paradise Garage.

nodes.name: Düsseldorf
nodes.description: Rhineland industrial city; home of Kraftwerk's Kling Klang studio.

nodes.name: Berlin
nodes.description: German city where club culture expanded after reunification and where Detroit techno circulated through record shops, clubs, labels, and artist exchanges. Berlin producers also developed distinct strands, including dub techno.

nodes.name: London
nodes.description: Sound-system capital where acid house became rave, and rave became a 30-year continuum.

nodes.name: I Feel Love
nodes.description: Donna Summer, produced by Giorgio Moroder — the first all-sequencer dance hit. Eno: 'This is the sound of the future.'

nodes.name: Clear
nodes.description: Cybotron's electro landmark: the exact midpoint between 'Planet Rock' and techno.

nodes.name: No UFO's
nodes.description: Model 500 (Juan Atkins), Metroplex M-001. Widely cited as the first techno record.

nodes.name: Strings of Life
nodes.description: Rhythim Is Rhythim (Derrick May). Piano stabs and strings with no bassline — techno's emotional anthem.

nodes.name: Acid Tracks
nodes.description: Phuture on Trax. Twelve minutes of TB-303 squelch that named and defined acid house.

nodes.name: Your Love
nodes.description: Frankie Knuckles and Jamie Principle — Chicago house's tenderest anthem.

nodes.name: The Warehouse

nodes.name: Techno
nodes.description: A family of electronic dance music first named and codified around Detroit in the mid-1980s, then developed through distinct scenes across the world. Repetitive machine rhythms and studio production are common reference points, while sound and social context vary widely.

nodes.name: Kelli Hand (K-HAND)
nodes.description: Detroit DJ and producer whose releases as K-HAND made her an important figure in the city’s house and techno communities. She was recognized for opening space for Black women in a male-dominated scene and continued recording and performing into her final years.

nodes.name: DJ Minx
nodes.description: Detroit DJ and producer active since the early 1990s. She founded the Women on Wax collective in 1996 and launched Women on Wax Recordings in 2001, creating platforms for women DJs and producers in the regional scene.

nodes.name: Women on Wax
nodes.description: A collective of women DJs from the Metro Detroit area founded by DJ Minx in 1996. Its work created a community and platform alongside the better-documented Detroit techno generations.

nodes.name: Mike “Mad Mike” Banks
nodes.description: Detroit producer and label operator who co-founded Underground Resistance with Jeff Mills. Banks helped shape the collective’s independent release network and its politically engaged second-generation techno work.

nodes.name: Underground Resistance
nodes.description: Detroit record label launched by Mike Banks and Jeff Mills in 1989, alongside the collective of the same name. It issued music by a changing roster of Detroit artists and built its own distribution and community infrastructure.

nodes.name: Women on Wax Recordings
nodes.description: Independent Detroit dance-music label founded by DJ Minx in 2001. It has released Minx’s work and music by local and international artists.

nodes.name: Techno City
nodes.description: Cybotron single first released in 1984; Juan Atkins used “techno” in the project’s musical vocabulary before the term became the name for the Detroit style.

nodes.name: French Touch
nodes.description: A Paris-centred electronic-music movement and export label of the late 1990s and early 2000s, spanning filter house, disco-inflected house, electro-pop and more. Scholarship treats it variously as a scene, a sound or a brand; it is broader than French house.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate international press, club and export visibility: French electronic music was already developing before the mid-1990s; Homework (1997) and late-1990s crossover singles made the label internationally prominent, while the first-wave formula had weakened by the mid-2000s. This is a scene history, not a sales curve.

nodes.name: French house
nodes.description: French-produced house associated with looped disco and funk samples, filtering and club production; it overlaps with but does not encompass the broader French Touch label.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate international club and press visibility: the style grew from early-1990s French production and reached a broad international profile around Homework, Cassius and Stardust in 1997–99. The phases describe one historical wave, not the ongoing reach of French house or all French Touch music.

nodes.name: Trip-hop
nodes.description: A press-coined label for downtempo, sample-based, jazz-, funk- and soul-inflected experimental breakbeat music associated with 1990s UK scenes. The Bristol Sound is related but not identical; Massive Attack, Portishead and Tricky have rejected the trip-hop label.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate UK press, album and critical visibility: the label spread in 1994–95 around landmark Bristol releases, and the mid-1990s were its clearest commercial/cultural moment. The label remained in use as artists moved on; the profile is not a measure of the Bristol scene or worldwide listening.

nodes.name: Big beat
nodes.description: A UK-led 1990s dance style built around forceful breakbeats, rock-scale dynamics, sampled hooks and rave energy; boundaries overlap with breaks and alternative dance.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate UK and international dance-chart visibility: Big Beat’s breakthrough gathered pace in the mid-1990s, peaked around late-1990s crossover records and receded as a named commercial wave in the early 2000s. Artists and breakbeat culture continued beyond this period.

nodes.name: Ambient
nodes.description: Electronic and electroacoustic music foregrounding atmosphere, timbre and space, often reducing or removing a regular beat. Its histories include several strands and are not a single linear descent.

nodes.name: Ambient techno
nodes.description: A dance-music formation combining techno/electro rhythmic frameworks with spacious ambient textures.

nodes.name: IDM / intelligent dance music
nodes.description: A 1990s label for experimental electronic listening music associated especially with Warp’s Artificial Intelligence releases; criticized as hierarchical, and many artists prefer other names.

nodes.name: Synthwave
nodes.description: An internet-mediated electronic genre reimagining 1980s film scores, synth-pop, game music and electronic production through nostalgic, cinematic synth textures. It emerged in the mid-2000s and gained visibility in the early 2010s.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial estimate of online-community growth and broader public visibility: synthwave formed online in the mid-to-late 2000s, with a marked visibility boost around Drive (2011), then diversified into continuing scenes. This is not a popularity ranking; global audience measures are unavailable.

nodes.name: Darksynth
nodes.description: A darker, heavier synthwave tendency using horror and dystopian imagery, harsher timbres and often industrial or metal inflections; its boundaries remain porous.

nodes.name: Vaporwave
nodes.description: An internet-born music and visual culture using slowed, looped and transformed samples—often commercial, lounge and corporate soundtrack material—to engage with consumerism, nostalgia and digital circulation.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial outline of online genre visibility: vaporwave emerged through internet releases and forums in the early 2010s, with a rapid viral/cultural moment around 2012–14, then continued in smaller, evolving communities. Not a measure of sales or all online activity.

nodes.name: Chillwave
nodes.description: A late-2000s/early-2010s online scene and style built around hazy production, reverb, softened vocals and nostalgic pop textures, overlapping with dream pop and synth-pop.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate U.S. blogosphere and indie-press visibility: the tag became prominent around 2009–10 and quickly faded as a press category, even as artists and related sounds continued. This describes a short-lived label wave, not an end to the music.

nodes.name: Downtempo
nodes.description: A broad umbrella for slower electronic music and listening-oriented arrangements, spanning ambient, chill-out, trip-hop and other distinct styles rather than one unified lineage.

nodes.name: Electroclash
nodes.description: A turn-of-the-millennium club scene combining electro, synth-pop/new wave references, punk attitude and theatrical performance; also a press and nightlife label.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate club, press and fashion visibility: the New York/European electroclash wave reached broad profile in the early 2000s before the label lost currency. Artists and related electro-pop styles persisted.

nodes.name: Breakbeat
nodes.description: A broad family of dance music organized around broken sampled or programmed drum breaks rather than a steady four-on-the-floor kick; fed hardcore, jungle and big beat.

nodes.name: Tech house
nodes.description: A club style combining house grooves and arrangements with techno’s stripped-down timbres and repetition; borders with minimal techno and progressive house shift across scenes.

nodes.name: Indie rock
nodes.description: Rock identity that grew from independent production and distribution networks into a broad stylistic category; musical conventions vary widely by scene and decade.

nodes.name: Garage rock
nodes.description: Raw, stripped-down rock associated with 1960s amateur and regional bands, drawing on rock and roll, blues and R&B; the name was later revived for new scenes.

nodes.name: Glam rock
nodes.description: Early-1970s British rock foregrounding theatrical performance, visual artifice, pop songwriting and amplified rock sounds.

nodes.name: Shoegaze
nodes.description: Late-1980s/early-1990s British indie rock marked by layered guitar effects, dense noise, blended vocals and introspective songwriting.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial outline of UK music-press visibility and later critical revival: the original scene is concentrated around the turn of the 1990s, followed by reappraisal and new waves from the 2000s onward. It is not a measure of record sales or global popularity.

nodes.name: Dream pop
nodes.description: Atmospheric melodic alternative pop/rock using effects, soft or blended vocals and spacious production; it overlaps with but is broader than shoegaze.

nodes.name: Britpop
nodes.description: British 1990s press and industry category for guitar pop/rock foregrounding British cultural references and melodic songwriting; membership and boundaries were debated.
nodes.phaseNote: Approximate UK chart and press visibility: Britpop’s broadest public moment was the mid-1990s, particularly 1994–96; the label and scene fragmented afterward. The shading is UK-centred and does not mark the end of British guitar music.

nodes.name: Emo
nodes.description: A family of rock styles originating in 1980s Washington, DC hardcore and expanding through 1990s indie and 2000s popular rock; meanings shifted substantially.

nodes.name: Post-hardcore
nodes.description: Diverse outgrowth of hardcore punk retaining intensity while exploring broader dynamics, structures and textures through distinct regional scenes.

nodes.name: Post-rock
nodes.description: Contested term for experimental rock using rock instrumentation while moving beyond conventional song forms, often toward texture, repetition or studio construction.

nodes.name: Math rock
nodes.description: Experimental rock associated with intricate irregular meters, angular guitar figures and tightly coordinated ensemble playing.

nodes.name: Noise rock
nodes.description: Abrasive rock foregrounding distortion, feedback, dissonance and unconventional performance; intersects post-punk, no wave and alternative rock.

nodes.name: Gothic rock
nodes.description: Post-punk development featuring dark atmospheres, dramatic vocals and romantic or alienation themes; goth music scene overlaps with but is not identical to goth subculture.

nodes.name: Pop-punk
nodes.description: Punk-derived rock pairing brisk tempos and power-chord energy with concise melodies and pop songwriting; later waves differ from early punk-pop.

nodes.name: Stoner rock
nodes.description: Heavy rock built around fuzzed guitar, low tunings, groove and extended riffs, drawing on hard rock, psychedelia and metal.

nodes.name: House
nodes.description: A post-disco electronic dance music tradition formed in Chicago club culture and developed through Black and queer DJs, producers and dancers. It became a global family of distinct local scenes and subgenres.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial outline of Chicago’s early scene formation and house’s spread into a larger international club culture. The shade is not a chart or global popularity measure.
